text: This is a stretch of interstate in central Indiana. Six lanes, paved shoulders, a grass median, a drainage inlet, a tree line, an overpass. Today it is mowed, swept, salted and patched. Now imagine every truck and every mower stops. Nobody drives it, nobody fixes it. What happens, season by season?

The first summer, the only change is at the edges. Nobody mows, so the shoulder grass goes to seed and leans over the white line. Mowing is what keeps a road's edge sharp. Without it, the edge is gone in one growing season.

The first fall, the trees along the right of way drop their leaves, and nobody sweeps. Wind piles them into the ditches and over the storm drains. A blocked drain is the first real failure. From now on, rain stays on the road instead of leaving it.

The first winter does the heavy work. Water sits in the small cracks that a road a few years old already has. When it freezes, ice grows and pushes the crack wider. When it thaws, more water gets in. Central Indiana sees roughly twenty-five to forty of these freeze and thaw swings a winter. That is a rough estimate; published counts depend on how you define a swing. Each one that catches water in the crack works it a little more open.

For a long time the explanation was simply that water expands about nine percent when it freezes. That number is right. But research published in twenty twenty-three found the stronger force is ice growing by pulling in more liquid water through tiny channels, the way frost heaves soil. Either way, nobody is sealing the crack, so each winter starts where the last one ended.

Years two to five. Rotting leaves and windblown dirt become a thin soil in the cracks, and seeds land in it. Moss and lichen come first, then grass and weeds. Water pools where the drains are blocked and softens the layers under the asphalt, and the first potholes can open. Engineers expect an asphalt surface to last about twenty years with maintenance. With none, and no one sealing the cracks, this simulation has it going faster.

Years five to twenty. Shrubs and tree seedlings move in from the tree lines. Maple, cottonwood, sumac, box elder, the kind of pioneers that take over an abandoned Indiana field. Birds and wind carry the seeds; deer and groundhogs dig at the soft shoulders. In the abandoned city of Pripyat, near Chernobyl, a survey published in twenty fifteen found streets so thick with young trees that some plots held nearly nine thousand Norway maple seedlings per hectare. Pavement slows this down; that survey still expects poplar and aspen to take the paved ground.

Lane paint fades within a few years. The steel sign posts rust from the ground line, and the sign leans. Roots lift the edges of the slabs. A grass fire in a dry year would burn off the dead stalks. Sumac resprouts after a fire; young cottonwood often does not. So a fire would not stop the trees, it would change which trees win.

Years twenty to fifty. Where there were lanes there is a young forest, and the old road shows as a line of broken slabs between the trees. On the overpass, water and road salt have reached the steel inside the concrete. Rust takes up several times the volume of the steel it came from, so it pushes the concrete off in flakes. That is spalling. Bridges are designed around a seventy-five-year life with inspections and repairs. Nobody is inspecting this one.

How long until it is all gone? Nobody knows exactly. This simulation is an estimate, built from studies of abandoned roads and cities. Abandoned paved roads in Puerto Rico had forest-like soil within about eleven years and forest structure after thirty. Pripyat has been empty since nineteen eighty-six, and its streets are woods now. In Indiana's climate, give or take, in fifty years you could walk past this stretch and not notice it was ever a highway. The road does not vanish because anything attacks it. It vanishes because nothing stops the small things.
A Heartbeat Observatory science short. Sources on screen.
